title: Q1: where do creatures come from? matter and breath (1)
hook: the first student asks where living things come from, and Pippalada answers with a pair: matter and breath, moon and sun
carry: the two paths of the sun
tomorrow: Q2: which gods hold the body?

segments.voice: Yesterday: six students, told to wait a year. Your line was earn the question. Did you carry a question a little longer before searching? The year is up. Day four hundred six, the end of week fifty-eight.

A year has passed. The six students have kept the discipline. And the first to step forward is Kabandhi Katyayana, with a question as old as asking. Sir, he says, from where are these creatures born? Children ask some version of it. Where did I come from? Where did the dog come from, the ants, the trees? A biologist would answer one way. A grandmother might answer another. Pippalada answers with a story, and at the center of the story is a pair, two things that need each other, the way a song needs both silence and sound.
screen: `THE YEAR IS UP.` → `SIR, WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?` → `THE ANSWER IS A PAIR.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, wanted offspring. He did tapas, the inner heat you met with Bhrigu. And from that heat he produced a pair: rayi and prana. Rayi means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form. Prana is breath, life, the energy that moves it. These two together, he thought, will make creatures for me. Then the pair shows up everywhere. The sun is prana. The moon is rayi. In a month, the dark half belongs to rayi, the bright half to prana. In a day, night is rayi, day is prana. Food, too, is Prajapati, because from food comes the seed from which creatures are born. Matter and life, always in pairs. Then the answer turns to people. The year itself, Pippalada says, is Prajapati, and it has two paths, a southern and a northern. Those who honor sacrifice and good works, digging wells, giving, keeping the rites, take the southern path, the path of the ancestors, to the world of the moon. And from there they return. Those who seek the self through tapas, a disciplined life, faith and knowledge, take the northern path, to the sun. That, the text says, is the resting place of breath, the immortal, the fearless. From there they do not return. So where do creatures come from? From matter meeting breath. And where do they go? The text names two paths, and what sets a person on either one is how they live.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TAPAS MAKES A PAIR.` · `RAYI IS MATTER; PRANA IS BREATH.` · `THE MOON AND THE SUN.` · `TWO PATHS: SOUTHERN AND NORTHERN.` · then, large: `RAYI AND PRANA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the pair. Sit, and feel the body's weight: bones, muscle, the pressure where you touch the chair or floor. That's rayi, matter, the moon side. Then feel the breath moving through it, warming it, lifting it. That's prana, the sun side. Let your attention rest on both at once: the stillness that holds and the motion that lives. Neither one is enough alone. The bell holds the time.
Rayi, wealth and matter, paired with prana, breath. Where do creatures come from? From rayi and prana, the moon and the sun, which Prajapati made as a pair.

Your line: the two paths of the sun. Today, notice your good works and your inner work, and give each one a few minutes. And that's week fifty-eight: the person, hunger and thirst, the door at the top, three births, the great saying, six students, and matter and breath. Day four hundred six.

howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the sun's northward turn at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and treat the northern half of the year, uttarayana, as an auspicious time, an idea that echoes the two paths of texts like this one.

myth: it means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form.
in the text, those on the southern path return
the path of the ancestors leads to the world of the moon, and back.
sir, from where are these creatures born?

fork.setup: Prajapati wants offspring. he does tapas. what does he make first?
fork.reveal: he makes rayi and prana, matter and breath, thinking these two together will make creatures for him.

original.note: Sanskrit rayi: wealth, substance, matter. paired with prāṇa, breath, in Prashna 1.4.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sun and moon are just sky decorations in old texts.
what it means: in the Prashna, the sun is breath and the moon is matter, and the year has two paths, one that returns and one that doesn't.
what a scholar hears: the southern path of the ancestors (pitryāna) and the northern path of the gods (devayāna) of Prashna 1.9–10 also appear in the Chandogya, Brihadaranyaka and Gita 8.24–25.
recall: the guest who comes without a set day

sources.ref: Prashna Upanishad 1.3–1.14 (rayi and prana; the two paths; month, day and night, food)

notes: Prashna 1.4–1.10 paraphrased from memory: rayi/prana; sun prana, moon rayi; dark half rayi, bright half prana; night rayi, day prana; food is Prajapati; southern path (ishtapurta, to the moon, return), northern path (tapas, brahmacharya, shraddha, vidya, to the sun, no return). Confirm order and the gloss 'digging wells' for purta.
